title: Homework 02
text:
TidyTuesday Part (Optional)
Explore the week’s TidyTuesday challenge. Develop a research question, then answer it through a short data story mainly composed of effective visualizations. Provide sufficient background for readers to grasp your narrative. Refer to the Homework Instructions ⭐ page on the course website for details on how to submit this part.
Codedead_scrolls<-read.csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-09-15/dead_sea_scrolls.csv')
Background The dead_scrolls dataset was curated by Tony Galvan of Golden Dome Data Science using information from the Israel Antiquities Authority’s official Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library. The dataset contains information about the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered near the Dead Sea. It includes variables such as the manuscript ID, the cave where the manuscript was found, the material it was made from, the discovery site, and the parent site.
I will use these variables to explore the types of texts found at different sites and consider what these texts may suggest about the beliefs and practices of the communities associated with those locations.
Codelibrary(tidyverse)

 # geom_point()+

  filter(composition!="Unidentified")|>
  group_by(composition)|>
  ggplot(aes(x=composition))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(title = "composition or biblical book identified ")
Codedead_scrolls|>
filter(composition!="Unidentified")|>
  group_by(site)

Codedead_scrolls|>
  ggplot(aes(x=language))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(title = "language of manuscript ")
Codedead_scrolls|>
  group_by(site_parent)|>
  ggplot(aes(x=site))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  labs(title = "full discovery site description ")
Codedead_scrolls|>
  ggplot(aes(x=biblical_book))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(title = "Identified Biblical book")
Codedead_scrolls|>
  filter(!bible_section=="Unidentified")|>
  ggplot(aes(x=bible_section))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(title = "bible section")
question What can the distribution of manuscripts found at different sites tell us about the types of texts associated with the beliefs of the commnunites around there?
Codedead_scrolls |>
  filter(content_category != "Unidentified") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = site_parent, fill = content_category)) +
  geom_bar() +
  geom_text(stat = "count",
    aes(label = after_stat(count)),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5))+
  labs(
    title = "Types of Texts Found Across Dead Sea Scrolls Sites",
    subtitle = "The Scarcity of Biblical Texts Suggests Broader Religious Traditions",
    x = "Discovery Site",
    y = "Number of Manuscripts",
    fill = "Content Category",
    caption = "Source: Week 2 TidyTuesday, Created on:09/20/26 by :Apiu Kur",
    alt = "A bar chart showing the number of manuscripts in different content categories at each Dead Sea Scrolls discovery site. The x-axis shows discovery sites and the y-axis shows the number of manuscripts. Different colors represent content categories."
  )
Codedead_scrolls|>
  ggplot(aes(x=num_images,y=site_parent,colour = content_category))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~testament)
_The Quamran communities contains the highest number of images taken to locate the specific manuscript _Qumran has a variety of the category of the books associated to them varying from Biblical,documentary,wisdom. -Masada had the wisdom literature. -Wadi Murabbat had a mix of biblical,Parabiblical -Nahal Hever had Biblical Liturgical -Masada mostly Biblical.
Codedead_scrolls|>
  ggplot(aes(x=num_images,y=site_parent,colour = testament))+
  geom_point()
#observations Qumran has a large number of manuscripts and contains a wide variety of text types. Many of the manuscripts found at Qumran are non-biblical, but the site also contains manuscripts of Old Testament texts. Masada also contains mostly non-biblical manuscripts. Across the sites, non-biblical texts make up a large part of the manuscripts, although the types of texts vary between locations.
The manuscripts found at different Dead Sea Scrolls sites provide clues about the kinds of texts that were important to the communities associated with those locations. Qumran stands out because it contains a large and diverse collection of manuscripts, including both biblical and non-biblical texts. The presence of Old Testament texts alongside other types of writings suggests that the community engaged with biblical traditions while also reading and producing other kinds of texts.
The large number of non-biblical manuscripts could mean that the communities had a broader range of beliefs, practices, laws, wisdom, and other ideas that were important to the communities.
